sermons.life_context: He was Fellow and Tutor in English at Magdalen College, Oxford, and lived at The Kilns in Headington Quarry, a household he shared with Janie Moore and, from 1932, his brother Warren. He had come to Christian belief in September 1931. This was his first sermon, preached about seven weeks after Britain declared war on Germany, when students and teachers were asking whether study was worth continuing (cslewis.com).

He was still Fellow and Tutor in English at Magdalen and living at The Kilns. Heck dates his first talk at an RAF station to 9 April 1941, two months before this sermon, and his first BBC broadcast came two months after it, on 6 August. This was his second sermon, again at the University Church.

While still teaching English at Magdalen and living at The Kilns, he travelled to London for these, his first BBC talks, two months after preaching 'The Weight of Glory'. He was also visiting RAF stations to speak during 1941–1943. According to cslewis.com, the BBC's James Welch invited him after reading The Problem of Pain.

A Magdalen tutor living at The Kilns, he gave these Sunday talks from London in the same weeks that the new Oxford University Socratic Club held its first meeting (26 January 1942), with him as its first president. He was also speaking at RAF stations (1941–1943), and The Screwtape Letters came out as a book in 1942.

Still a Magdalen tutor living at The Kilns, he gave this lay talk in London during his third BBC series, Christian Behaviour, and broadcast on social morality the same day (Heck). Earlier in 1942 he had become first president of the Oxford University Socratic Club, and The Screwtape Letters was published as a book that year.

While teaching at Magdalen and living at The Kilns, he gave this third BBC series from London in autumn 1942, the year he became first president of the Oxford University Socratic Club and The Screwtape Letters appeared as a book. Early in the run, on 27 September, he also gave a lay talk at St Jude on the Hill, Hampstead (Heck).

Still a Magdalen tutor living at The Kilns, he gave this fourth and final series of BBC talks in early 1944, recording some of them in advance (Heck). His visits to speak at RAF stations, begun in 1941, had run through 1943.

Still Fellow and Tutor in English at Magdalen and living at The Kilns in Oxford, he travelled to London for this college oration in the last full year of the war, about eight months after his fourth and final BBC series ended in April 1944.

sermons.life_context: Still a Magdalen tutor living at The Kilns, he gave this London talk about three weeks before the war in Europe ended on 8 May 1945, and two days after The Guardian printed the last instalment of The Great Divorce. Brenton Dickieson places it among pieces written while he was developing his book Miracles (1947).

sermons.life_context: He was still Fellow and Tutor in English at Magdalen and living at The Kilns in Headington Quarry. A week earlier, on 31 March 1946, he had preached what Heck takes to be a version of this sermon at Evensong at Holy Trinity, Headington Quarry; cslewis.com says the message was the same on both occasions.

The year is disputed. If it was 28 May 1944, he was a Magdalen tutor living at The Kilns, weeks after his fourth and final BBC series ended in April. If it was 9 June 1946 (Heck's date), he was still at Magdalen, two months after preaching 'Miserable Offenders' at Headington Quarry and Northampton.

A year into his Cambridge chair of Medieval and Renaissance English, with a fellowship at Magdalene College, he spent term weeks in Cambridge and went home to The Kilns in Oxford between terms. Less than three months later, on 23 April 1956, he married Joy Davidman in a civil ceremony in Oxford that secured her right to remain in Britain.

He was Professor of Medieval and Renaissance English at Cambridge and a fellow of Magdalene College, dividing his time between Cambridge in term and The Kilns in Oxford. He had married Joy Davidman in a civil ceremony in 1956, followed in March 1957 by a church ceremony at her Oxford hospital bedside after she was found to have cancer.
